Built for speed Fast animals share the same engineering: a streamlined body, oversized heart and lungs, and muscles loaded with fast-twitch fibres. The cheetah adds a flexible spine that lengthens its stride, semi-retractable claws that work like running spikes, and a long tail for steering. The peregrine adds baffles in its nostrils that slow incoming air so a 300+ km/h dive doesn't damage its lungs. Fastest animals: FAQs What is the fastest animal in the world? The peregrine falcon. In a hunting dive (called a stoop) it reaches around 389 km/h (242 mph) — more than three times the cheetah's top running speed and faster than most sports cars on a motorway. What is the fastest land animal? The cheetah, at around 110 km/h (68 mph) in short bursts over a few hundred metres. It cannot sustain that pace for long — most chases are over in under a minute. In addition to GPS and radar, researchers have also studied the biomechanics of cheetah movement through high-speed cameras. These cameras capture the cheetah's running style in detail, allowing scientists to analyse its stride pattern and the mechanics of its limbs. This research has revealed that cheetahs can change direction rapidly while maintaining speed, an essential skill for hunting in the wild. The combination of speed, agility, and the ability to make quick turns is what sets the cheetah apart from other fast land animals. Other Fast Land Animals While the cheetah is the fastest land animal, several other species exhibit impressive speeds. The pronghorn (Antilocapra americana), native to North America, is the second fastest, capable of reaching speeds up to 88 km/h (55 mph). Unlike cheetahs, pronghorns can sustain high speeds over longer distances, making them formidable runners in their own right. The sailfish is commonly cited as the fastest fish, at around 110 km/h (68 mph) in short bursts. In our own guide the swordfish is the fastest profiled fish, listed at 80 km/h (50 mph). Why are birds faster than land animals? Two reasons: diving and aerodynamics. A falcon in a stoop is essentially falling with control, converting gravity into speed while tucking its wings to minimise drag. Even in level flight, air offers far less resistance than the ground, and wings avoid the obstacles that limit running animals.

For example, the gazelle's ability to make sharp turns at high speeds helps it evade predators like lions and cheetahs. In contrast, the pronghorn's endurance allows it to escape over vast distances, showcasing the different evolutionary paths taken by these fast land animals. Additionally, the greyhound (Canis lupus familiaris) is often cited as one of the fastest dog breeds, capable of reaching speeds of 72 km/h (45 mph). While not a wild animal, greyhounds have been bred for speed and agility in racing contexts. Their slender bodies and long legs are similar to those of the cheetah, illustrating how speed has been a desirable trait in both wild and domesticated species. The adaptations seen in these animals reflect the evolutionary pressures they face in their respective environments. The Role of Speed in Survival Speed plays a critical role in the survival of many species in the wild. For predators like the cheetah, speed is essential for hunting. The ability to sprint quickly allows them to catch agile prey, while their unique adaptations help them maximise their hunting success.

passages.text: Fastest animals This is a list of the fastest animals in the world, by types of animal. The peregrine falcon is the fastest bird, and the fastest member of the animal kingdom, with a diving speed of over 300 km/h (190 mph).[1] The fastest land animal is the cheetah, capable of running at speeds of up to 93–104 km/h (58–65 mph). Among the fastest animals in the sea is the black marlin, with uncertain and conflicting reports of recorded speeds.[2][3] When drawing comparisons between different classes of animals, an alternative unit is sometimes used for organisms: body length per second. On this basis the 'fastest' organism on earth, relative to its body length, is the Southern Californian mite, Paratarsotomus macropalpis, which has a speed of 322 body lengths per second.[4] The equivalent speed for a human, running as fast as this mite, would be 1,300 mph (2,092 km/h),[5] or approximately Mach 1.7.
